newsitem.title: USA: US DOE may separate Northwest in electricity bill.
newsitem.headline: US DOE may separate Northwest in electricity bill.

text.p: The Clinton administration likely will treat the Pacific Northwest region, with its heavy reliance on the Bonneville Power Administration, separately in its electricity deregulation proposal, Acting Energy Secretary Charles Curtis said Tuesday.

Appearing before the House Commerce Energy and Power subcommittee, Energy Department officials also said they would like to negotiate with Congress to find alternatives to selling some 50 million barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to help balance the federal budget in 2002.

"We will likely be inclined to favor addressing the Northwest separately in legislation as it deals with these very important and sensitive issues" in electricity restructuring legislation, Curtis said.
A number of Northwestern congressmen have said they would vehemently oppose any efforts to privatize Bonneville in the plan to increase competitiveness in the nation's electric power industry.
Curtis restated that he knew of no plans in the administration to sell or privatize Bonneville.

Responding to questions on whether the Energy Department endorsed the White House's proposed sale of $1.1 billion, or roughly 50 million barrels, of oil from the SPR in fiscal 2002 to help balance the budget, Associate Deputy Energy Secretary Kyle Simpson said he hoped Congress would help find ways to avoid the sale.

With the differences in budget projections between the Congressional Budget Office and the White House Office of Management and Budget, Simpson said the administration and Congress may find other ways to meet budget projections.
"We would be very willing to work with the Congress...with the goal to eliminate that sale," Simpson said.
Subcommittee Chairman Dan Schaefer, a Colorado Republican, has sharply criticized the proposed sale, saying it could detract from the nation's energy security.

Also at the hearing, several subcommittee members criticized the administration for not offering a plan on how to deal with the government's responsibility to start accepting spent fuel from nuclear reactors, and said the administration did not seek enough money in its fiscal 1998 budget plan to deal with the problem.
